# wasmtime_cranelift - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime-cranelift/

## Expand description

Support for compiling with Cranelift.

This crate provides an implementation of the `wasmtime_environ::Compiler`
and `wasmtime_environ::CompilerBuilder` traits.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Compiled](https://docs.rs/struct.CompiledFunction.html)- Function
- Compiled function: machine code body, jump table offsets, and unwind information.
- [Compiled](https://docs.rs/struct.CompiledFunctionMetadata.html)- Function - Metadata
- The metadata for the compiled function.
- [Function](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionAddressMap.html)- Address - Map
- Metadata to translate from binary offsets back to the original location found in the wasm input.
- [Module](https://docs.rs/struct.ModuleTextBuilder.html)- Text - Builder
- A helper structure used to assemble the final text section of an executable, plus unwinding information and other related details.
- [Relocation](https://docs.rs/struct.Relocation.html)
- A record of a relocation to perform.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [NS_](https://docs.rs/constant.NS_PULLEY_HOSTCALL.html)- PULLEY_ - HOSTCALL
- Namespace used to when a call from Pulley to the host is being made. This is
used with a `colocated: false`name to trigger codegen for a special opcode for pulley-to-host communication. The index of the functions used in this namespace correspond to the function signature of`for_each_host_signature!`in the pulley_interpreter crate.
- [NS_](https://docs.rs/constant.NS_WASMTIME_BUILTIN.html)- WASMTIME_ - BUILTIN
- Namespace for builtin function trampolines. The index is the index of the
builtin that’s being referenced. These trampolines invoke the real host
function through an indirect function call loaded by the `VMContext`.
- [NS_](https://docs.rs/constant.NS_WASM_FUNC.html)- WASM_ - FUNC
- Namespace corresponding to wasm functions, the index is the index of the defined function that’s being referenced.
- [TRAP_](https://docs.rs/constant.TRAP_ALLOCATION_TOO_LARGE.html)- ALLOCATION_ - TOO_ - LARGE
- [TRAP_](https://docs.rs/constant.TRAP_ALWAYS.html)- ALWAYS
- [TRAP_](https://docs.rs/constant.TRAP_ARRAY_OUT_OF_BOUNDS.html)- ARRAY_ - OUT_ - OF_ - BOUNDS
- [TRAP_](https://docs.rs/constant.TRAP_BAD_SIGNATURE.html)- BAD_ - SIGNATURE
- [TRAP_](https://docs.rs/constant.TRAP_CANNOT_ENTER.html)- CANNOT_ - ENTER
- [TRAP_](https://docs.rs/constant.TRAP_CAST_FAILURE.html)- CAST_ - FAILURE
- [TRAP_](https://docs.rs/constant.TRAP_HEAP_MISALIGNED.html)- HEAP_ - MISALIGNED
- [TRAP_](https://docs.rs/constant.TRAP_INDIRECT_CALL_TO_NULL.html)- INDIRECT_ - CALL_ - TO_ - NULL
- [TRAP_](https://docs.rs/constant.TRAP_NULL_REFERENCE.html)- NULL_ - REFERENCE
- [TRAP_](https://docs.rs/constant.TRAP_TABLE_OUT_OF_BOUNDS.html)- TABLE_ - OUT_ - OF_ - BOUNDS
- [TRAP_](https://docs.rs/constant.TRAP_UNREACHABLE.html)- UNREACHABLE

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [builder](https://docs.rs/fn.builder.html)
- [clif_](https://docs.rs/fn.clif_flags_to_wasmtime.html)- flags_ - to_ - wasmtime
- Converts cranelift_codegen settings to the wasmtime_environ equivalent.
- [mach_](https://docs.rs/fn.mach_trap_to_trap.html)- trap_ - to_ - trap
- Converts machine traps to trap information.

# anyhow - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/anyhow/^1.0.93/

## Expand description

This library provides [ anyhow::Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html), a trait object based error
type for easy idiomatic error handling in Rust applications.

[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

-
Use `Result<T, anyhow::Error>`, or equivalently`anyhow::Result<T>`, as the return type of any fallible function.Within the function, use `?`to easily propagate any error that implements the`std::error::Error``use anyhow::Result; fn get_cluster_info() -> Result<ClusterMap> { let config = std::fs::read_to_string("cluster.json")?; let map: ClusterMap = serde_json::from_str(&config)?; Ok(map) }`
-
Attach context to help the person troubleshooting the error understand where things went wrong. A low-level error like “No such file or directory” can be annoying to debug without more context about what higher level step the application was in the middle of. `use anyhow::{Context, Result}; fn main() -> Result<()> { ... it.detach().context("Failed to detach the important thing")?; let content = std::fs::read(path) .with_context(|| format!("Failed to read instrs from {}", path))?; ... }``Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json Caused by: No such file or directory (os error 2)`
-
Downcasting is supported and can be by value, by shared reference, or by mutable reference as needed. `// If the error was caused by redaction, then return a // tombstone instead of the content. match root_cause.downcast_ref::<DataStoreError>() { Some(DataStoreError::Censored(_)) => Ok(Poll::Ready(REDACTED_CONTENT)), None => Err(error), }`
-
If using Rust ≥ 1.65, a backtrace is captured and printed with the error if the underlying error type does not already provide its own. In order to see backtraces, they must be enabled through the environment variables described in `std::backtrace`- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
`RUST_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only errors to have backtraces, set `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only panics to have backtraces, set `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`and`RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0`.

- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
-
Anyhow works with any error type that has an impl of `std::error::Error`, including ones defined in your crate. We do not bundle a`derive(Error)`macro but you can write the impls yourself or use a standalone macro like[thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror).`use thiserror::Error; #[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum FormatError { #[error("Invalid header (expected {expected:?}, got {found:?})")] InvalidHeader { expected: String, found: String, }, #[error("Missing attribute: {0}")] MissingAttribute(String), }`
-
One-off error messages can be constructed using the `anyhow!`macro, which supports string interpolation and produces an`anyhow::Error`.`return Err(anyhow!("Missing attribute: {}", missing));`A `bail!`macro is provided as a shorthand for the same early return.`bail!("Missing attribute: {}", missing);`

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

In no_std mode, almost all of the same API is available and works the same way. To depend on Anyhow in no_std mode, disable our default enabled “std” feature in Cargo.toml. A global allocator is required.

```
[dependencies]
anyhow = { version = "1.0", default-features = false }
```
With versions of Rust older than 1.81, no_std mode may require an additional
`.map_err(Error::msg)` when working with a non-Anyhow error type inside a
function that returns Anyhow’s error type, as the trait that `?`-based error
conversions are defined by is only available in std in those old versions.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [anyhow](https://docs.rs/macro.anyhow.html)as format_err;

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [anyhow](https://docs.rs/macro.anyhow.html)
- Construct an ad-hoc error from a string or existing non-`anyhow`error value.
- [bail](https://docs.rs/macro.bail.html)
- Return early with an error.
- [ensure](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html)
- Return early with an error if a condition is not satisfied.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Chain](https://docs.rs/struct.Chain.html)
- Iterator of a chain of source errors.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- The `Error`type, a wrapper around a dynamic error type.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Context](https://docs.rs/trait.Context.html)
- Provides the `context`method for`Result`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [Ok](https://docs.rs/fn.Ok.html)
- Equivalent to `Ok::<_, anyhow::Error>(value)`.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- `Result<T, Error>`

# cfg_if - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cfg-if/^1.0/

## Expand description

A macro for defining `#[cfg]` if-else statements.

The macro provided by this crate, `cfg_if`, is similar to the `if/elif` C
preprocessor macro by allowing definition of a cascade of `#[cfg]` cases,
emitting the implementation which matches first.

This allows you to conveniently provide a long list `#[cfg]`’d blocks of code
without having to rewrite each clause multiple times.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
cfg_if::cfg_if! {
    if #[cfg(unix)] {
        fn foo() { /* unix specific functionality */ }
    } else if #[cfg(target_pointer_width = "32")] {
        fn foo() { /* non-unix, 32-bit functionality */ }
    } else {
        fn foo() { /* fallback implementation */ }
    }
}
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [cfg_if](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_if.html)
- The main macro provided by this crate. See crate documentation for more information.

---

- [Call](https://docs.rs/struct.CallInfo.html)- Info

- Status of a compiled artifact ready to use.

- A buffer of output to be produced, fixed up, and then emitted to a CodeSink in bulk.
- [Mach](https://docs.rs/struct.MachBufferFinalized.html)- Buffer - Finalized
- A `MachBuffer`once emission is completed: holds generated code and records, without fixups. This allows the type to be independent of the backend.
- [Mach](https://docs.rs/struct.MachCallSite.html)- Call - Site
- A call site record resulting from a compilation.
- [Mach](https://docs.rs/struct.MachLabel.html)- Label
- A label refers to some offset in a `MachBuffer`. It may not be resolved at the point at which it is used by emitted code; the buffer records “fixups” for references to the label, and will come back and patch the code appropriately when the label’s location is eventually known.
- [Mach](https://docs.rs/struct.MachSrcLoc.html)- SrcLoc
- A source-location mapping resulting from a compilation.
- [Mach](https://docs.rs/struct.MachTextSectionBuilder.html)- Text - Section - Builder
- Implementation of the `TextSectionBuilder`trait backed by`MachBuffer`.
- [Mach](https://docs.rs/struct.MachTrap.html)- Trap
- A trap record resulting from a compilation.
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenPatchRegion.html)- Patch - Region
- Represents the beginning of an editable region in the `MachBuffer``OpenPatchRegion``MachBuffer::end_patchable``OpenPatchRegion`
- [Patch](https://docs.rs/struct.PatchRegion.html)- Region
- A region in the `MachBuffer``MachBuffer::start_patchable``PatchRegion``MachBuffer::end_patchable``PatchRegion::patch`
- [RealReg](https://docs.rs/struct.RealReg.html)
- A real (physical) register. This corresponds to one of the target ISA’s named registers and can be used as an instruction operand.
- [Reg](https://docs.rs/struct.Reg.html)
- A register named in an instruction. This register can be a virtual
register, a fixed physical register, or a named spillslot (after
regalloc). It does not have any constraints applied to it: those
can be added later in `MachInst::get_operands()`when the`Reg`s are converted to`Operand`s.
- [Take](https://docs.rs/struct.TakeAndReplace.html)- AndReplace
- An RAII type to temporarily take a `U`out of a`T`and then put it back again on drop.
- [VCode](https://docs.rs/struct.VCodeConstant.html)- Constant
- A use of a constant by one or more VCode instructions; see [VCodeConstants](https://docs.rs/struct.VCodeConstants.html).
- [VCode](https://docs.rs/struct.VCodeConstants.html)- Constants
- This structure tracks the large constants used in VCode that will be emitted separately by the
[MachBuffer](https://docs.rs/struct.MachBuffer.html).
- [Value](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueLocRange.html)- LocRange
- Value location range.
- [Writable](https://docs.rs/struct.Writable.html)
- A type wrapper that indicates a register type is writable. The
underlying register can be extracted, and the type wrapper can be
built using an arbitrary register. Hence, this type-level wrapper
is not strictly a guarantee. However, “casting” to a writable
register is an explicit operation for which we can
audit. Ordinarily, internal APIs in the compiler backend should
take a `Writable<Reg>`whenever the register is written, and the usual, frictionless way to get one of these is to allocate a new temporary.

# cranelift_control - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-control/^0.121.2/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#cranelift-control)Cranelift Control

This is the home of the control plane of chaos mode, a compilation feature
intended to be turned on for certain fuzz targets. When the feature is
turned off, as is normally the case, [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html) will be a zero-sized
type and optimized away.

While the feature is turned on, the struct [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html)
provides functionality to tap into pseudo-randomness at specific locations
in the code. It may be used for targeted fuzzing of compiler internals,
e.g. manipulate heuristic optimizations, clobber undefined register bits
etc.

There are two ways to acquire a [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html):

- [arbitrary](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html#method.arbitrary)for the real deal (requires the- `fuzz`feature, enabled by default)
- [default](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html#method.default)for an “empty” control plane which always returns default values

[§](https://docs.rs#fuel-limit)Fuel Limit

Controls the number of mutations or optimizations that the compiler will perform before stopping.

When a perturbation introduced by chaos mode triggers a bug, it may not be immediately clear which of the introduced perturbations was the trigger. The fuel limit can then be used to binary-search for the trigger. It limits the number of perturbations introduced by the control plane. The fuel limit will typically be set with a command line argument passed to a fuzz target. For example:

`cargo fuzz run --features chaos $TARGET -- --fuel=16`[§](https://docs.rs#no_std-support)`no_std` support

This crate compiles in `no_std` environments, although both the `fuzz`
or `chaos` features have a dependency on `std`. This means that on `no_std`
you can’t use [arbitrary](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html#method.arbitrary) to initialize [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html) and can’t enable
chaos mode, although the rest of the usual [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html) API is available.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Control](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html)- Plane
- A shim for ControlPlane when chaos mode is disabled.
Please see the [crate-level documentation](https://docs.rs/index.html).

---

# cranelift_entity - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-entity/^0.121.2/

## Expand description

Array-based data structures using densely numbered entity references as mapping keys.

This crate defines a number of data structures based on arrays. The arrays are not indexed by
`usize` as usual, but by *entity references* which are integers wrapped in new-types. This has
a couple advantages:

- Improved type safety. The various map and set types accept a specific key type, so there is no confusion about the meaning of an array index, as there is with plain arrays.
- Smaller indexes. The normal `usize`index is often 64 bits which is way too large for most purposes. The entity reference types can be smaller, allowing for more compact data structures.

The `EntityRef` trait should be implemented by types to be used as indexed. The `entity_impl!`
macro provides convenient defaults for types wrapping `u32` which is common.

- `PrimaryMap`
- `SecondaryMap`
- `SparseMap`
- `EntitySet`
- `EntityList`- `Vec`.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [packed_](https://docs.rs/packed_option/index.html)- option
- Compact representation of `Option<T>`for types with a reserved value.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [entity_](https://docs.rs/macro.entity_impl.html)- impl
- Macro which provides the common implementation of a 32-bit entity reference.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Boxed](https://docs.rs/struct.BoxedSlice.html)- Slice
- A slice mapping `K -> V`allocating dense entity references.
- [Entity](https://docs.rs/struct.EntityList.html)- List
- A small list of entity references allocated from a pool.
- [Entity](https://docs.rs/struct.EntitySet.html)- Set
- A set of `K`for densely indexed entity references.
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- Iterate over all keys in order.
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.IterEntityRange.html)- Entity - Range
- Iterator type returned by `iter_entity_range`.
- [IterMut](https://docs.rs/struct.IterMut.html)
- Iterate over all keys in order.
- [Keys](https://docs.rs/struct.Keys.html)
- Iterate over all keys in order.
- [List](https://docs.rs/struct.ListPool.html)- Pool
- A memory pool for storing lists of `T`.
- [Primary](https://docs.rs/struct.PrimaryMap.html)- Map
- A primary mapping `K -> V`allocating dense entity references.
- [Secondary](https://docs.rs/struct.SecondaryMap.html)- Map
- A mapping `K -> V`for densely indexed entity references.
- [SetIter](https://docs.rs/struct.SetIter.html)
- An iterator over the elements in an `EntitySet`.
- [Sparse](https://docs.rs/struct.SparseMap.html)- Map
- A sparse mapping of entity references.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Entity](https://docs.rs/trait.EntityRef.html)- Ref
- A type wrapping a small integer index should implement `EntityRef`so it can be used as the key of an`SecondaryMap`or`SparseMap`.
- [Signed](https://docs.rs/trait.Signed.html)
- Helper trait used to add `signed()`methods to primitive unsigned integer types.
- [Sparse](https://docs.rs/trait.SparseMapValue.html)- MapValue
- Trait for extracting keys from values stored in a `SparseMap`.
- [Unsigned](https://docs.rs/trait.Unsigned.html)
- Helper trait used to add `unsigned()`methods to primitive signed integer types.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [iter_](https://docs.rs/fn.iter_entity_range.html)- entity_ - range
- Iterate over a `Range<E: EntityRef>`, yielding a sequence of`E`items.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- A sparse set of entity references.

# cranelift_frontend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-frontend/^0.121.2/

## Expand description

Cranelift IR builder library.

Provides a straightforward way to create a Cranelift IR function and fill it with instructions corresponding to your source program written in another language.

To get started, create an [ FunctionBuilderContext](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionBuilderContext.html) and
pass it as an argument to a

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionBuilder.html)

`FunctionBuilder`[§](https://docs.rs#mutable-variables-and-cranelift-ir-values)Mutable variables and Cranelift IR values

The most interesting feature of this API is that it provides a single way to deal with all your
variable problems. Indeed, the [ FunctionBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionBuilder.html) struct has a
type

`Variable` that should be an index of your source language variables. Then, through
calling the functions
[,](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionBuilder.html#method.declare_var)

`declare_var`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionBuilder.html#method.def_var)

`def_var`[, the](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionBuilder.html#method.use_var)

`use_var`[will create for you all the Cranelift IR values corresponding to your variables.](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionBuilder.html)

`FunctionBuilder`This API has been designed to help you translate your mutable variables into
[ SSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Static_single_assignment_form) form.

[will return the Cranelift IR value that corresponds to your mutable variable at a precise point in the program. However, if you know beforehand that one of your variables is defined only once, for instance if it is the result of an intermediate expression in an expression-based language, then you can translate it directly by the Cranelift IR value returned by the instruction builder. Using the](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionBuilder.html#method.use_var)

`use_var`[API for such an immutable variable would also work but with a slight additional overhead (the SSA algorithm does not know beforehand if a variable is immutable or not).](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionBuilder.html#method.use_var)

`use_var`The moral is that you should use these three functions to handle all your mutable variables,
even those that are not present in the source code but artifacts of the translation. It is up
to you to keep a mapping between the mutable variables of your language and their [ Variable](https://docs.rs/struct.Variable.html)
index that is used by Cranelift. Caution: as the

[is used by Cranelift to index an array containing information about your mutable variables, when you create a new](https://docs.rs/struct.Variable.html)

`Variable`[with](https://docs.rs/struct.Variable.html)

`Variable``Variable::new(var_index)` you should make sure that `var_index`
is provided by a counter incremented by 1 each time you encounter a new mutable variable.[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Here is a pseudo-program we want to transform into Cranelift IR:

```
function(x) {
x, y, z : i32
block0:
   y = 2;
   z = x + y;
   jump block1
block1:
   z = z + y;
   brif y, block3, block2
block2:
   z = z - x;
   return y
block3:
   y = y - x
   jump block1
}
```
Here is how you build the corresponding Cranelift IR function using [ FunctionBuilderContext](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionBuilderContext.html):

```
use cranelift_codegen::entity::EntityRef;
use cranelift_codegen::ir::types::*;
use cranelift_codegen::ir::{AbiParam, UserFuncName, Function, InstBuilder, Signature};
use cranelift_codegen::isa::CallConv;
use cranelift_codegen::settings;
use cranelift_codegen::verifier::verify_function;
use cranelift_frontend::{FunctionBuilder, FunctionBuilderContext, Variable};
let mut sig = Signature::new(CallConv::SystemV);
sig.returns.push(AbiParam::new(I32));
sig.params.push(AbiParam::new(I32));
let mut fn_builder_ctx = FunctionBuilderContext::new();
let mut func = Function::with_name_signature(UserFuncName::user(0, 0), sig);
{
    let mut builder = FunctionBuilder::new(&mut func, &mut fn_builder_ctx);
    let block0 = builder.create_block();
    let block1 = builder.create_block();
    let block2 = builder.create_block();
    let block3 = builder.create_block();
    let x = Variable::new(0);
    let y = Variable::new(1);
    let z = Variable::new(2);
    builder.declare_var(x, I32);
    builder.declare_var(y, I32);
    builder.declare_var(z, I32);
    builder.append_block_params_for_function_params(block0);
    builder.switch_to_block(block0);
    builder.seal_block(block0);
    {
        let tmp = builder.block_params(block0)[0]; // the first function parameter
        builder.def_var(x, tmp);
    }
    {
        let tmp = builder.ins().iconst(I32, 2);
        builder.def_var(y, tmp);
    }
    {
        let arg1 = builder.use_var(x);
        let arg2 = builder.use_var(y);
        let tmp = builder.ins().iadd(arg1, arg2);
        builder.def_var(z, tmp);
    }
    builder.ins().jump(block1, &[]);
    builder.switch_to_block(block1);
    {
        let arg1 = builder.use_var(y);
        let arg2 = builder.use_var(z);
        let tmp = builder.ins().iadd(arg1, arg2);
        builder.def_var(z, tmp);
    }
    {
        let arg = builder.use_var(y);
        builder.ins().brif(arg, block3, &[], block2, &[]);
    }
    builder.switch_to_block(block2);
    builder.seal_block(block2);
    {
        let arg1 = builder.use_var(z);
        let arg2 = builder.use_var(x);
        let tmp = builder.ins().isub(arg1, arg2);
        builder.def_var(z, tmp);
    }
    {
        let arg = builder.use_var(y);
        builder.ins().return_(&[arg]);
    }
    builder.switch_to_block(block3);
    builder.seal_block(block3);
    {
        let arg1 = builder.use_var(y);
        let arg2 = builder.use_var(x);
        let tmp = builder.ins().isub(arg1, arg2);
        builder.def_var(y, tmp);
    }
    builder.ins().jump(block1, &[]);
    builder.seal_block(block1);
    builder.finalize();
}
let flags = settings::Flags::new(settings::builder());
let res = verify_function(&func, &flags);
println!("{}", func.display());
if let Err(errors) = res {
    panic!("{}", errors);
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- Implementation of the `InstBuilder`
- [Function](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionBuilder.html)- Builder
- Temporary object used to build a single Cranelift IR `Function`
- [Function](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionBuilderContext.html)- Builder - Context
- Structure used for translating a series of functions into Cranelift IR.

- Unlike with `br_table`,`Switch`cases may be sparse or non-0-based. They emit efficient code using branches, jump tables, or a combination of both.
- [Variable](https://docs.rs/struct.Variable.html)
- An opaque reference to a variable.

- Version number of this crate.

# gimli - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/gimli/^0.31.0/

## Expand description

`gimli` is a library for reading and writing the
[DWARF debugging format](https://dwarfstd.org/).

See the [read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html) and [write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html) modules
for examples and API documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

Cargo features that can be enabled with `gimli`:

-
`std`: Enabled by default. Use the`std`library. Disabling this feature allows using`gimli`in embedded environments that do not have access to`std`. Note that even when`std`is disabled,`gimli`still requires an implementation of the`alloc`crate.
-
`read`: Enabled by default. Enables the`read`module. Use of`std`is optional.
-
`write`: Enabled by default. Enables the`write`module. Always uses the`std`library.

- Read and write DWARF’s “Little Endian Base 128” (LEB128) variable length integer encoding.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Clone](https://docs.rs/trait.CloneStableDeref.html)- Stable - Deref
- An unsafe marker trait for types where clones deref to the same address. This has all the requirements of StableDeref, and additionally requires that after calling clone(), both the old and new value deref to the same address. For example, Rc and Arc implement CloneStableDeref, but Box and Vec do not.
- [Endianity](https://docs.rs/trait.Endianity.html)
- A trait describing the endianity of some buffer.
- [Stable](https://docs.rs/trait.StableDeref.html)- Deref
- An unsafe marker trait for types that deref to a stable address, even when moved. For example, this is implemented by Box, Vec, Rc, Arc and String, among others. Even when a Box is moved, the underlying storage remains at a fixed location.

# itertools - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/itertools/^0.14.0/

## Expand description

Extra iterator adaptors, functions and macros.

To extend [ Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html) with methods in this crate, import
the

[trait:](https://docs.rs/trait.Itertools.html)

`Itertools``use itertools::Itertools;`Now, new methods like [ interleave](https://docs.rs/trait.Itertools.html#method.interleave)
are available on all iterators:

```
use itertools::Itertools;
let it = (1..3).interleave(vec![-1, -2]);
itertools::assert_equal(it, vec![1, -1, 2, -2]);
```
Most iterator methods are also provided as functions (with the benefit
that they convert parameters using [ IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)):

```
use itertools::interleave;
for elt in interleave(&[1, 2, 3], &[2, 3, 4]) {
    /* loop body */
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate Features

- `use_std`- Enabled by default.
- Disable to compile itertools using `#![no_std]`. This disables any item that depend on allocations (see the`use_alloc`feature) and hash maps (like`unique`,`counts`,`into_grouping_map`and more).

- `use_alloc`- Enabled by default.
- Enables any item that depend on allocations (like `chunk_by`,`kmerge`,`join`and many more).

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version)Rust Version

This version of itertools requires Rust 1.63.0 or later.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::`- [structs](https://docs.rs/structs/index.html)::*;

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [merge](https://docs.rs/fn.merge.html)
- Create an iterator that merges elements in `i`and`j`.
- [merge_](https://docs.rs/fn.merge_join_by.html)- join_ - by
- Return an iterator adaptor that merge-joins items from the two base iterators in ascending order.
- [min](https://docs.rs/fn.min.html)
- Return the minimum value of the iterable.
- [multipeek](https://docs.rs/fn.multipeek.html)
- An iterator adaptor that allows the user to peek at multiple `.next()`values without advancing the base iterator.
- [multiunzip](https://docs.rs/fn.multiunzip.html)
- Converts an iterator of tuples into a tuple of containers.
- [multizip](https://docs.rs/fn.multizip.html)
- An iterator that generalizes `.zip()`and allows running multiple iterators in lockstep.
- [partition](https://docs.rs/fn.partition.html)
- Partition a sequence using predicate `pred`so that elements that map to`true`are placed before elements which map to`false`.
- [peek_](https://docs.rs/fn.peek_nth.html)- nth
- A drop-in replacement for `std::iter::Peekable``peek_nth`method allowing the user to`peek`at a value several iterations forward without advancing the base iterator.
- [process_](https://docs.rs/fn.process_results.html)- results
- “Lift” a function of the values of an iterator so that it can process
an iterator of `Result`values instead.
- [put_](https://docs.rs/fn.put_back.html)- back
- Create an iterator where you can put back a single item
- [put_](https://docs.rs/fn.put_back_n.html)- back_ - n
- Create an iterator where you can put back multiple values to the front of the iteration.
- [rciter](https://docs.rs/fn.rciter.html)
- Return an iterator inside a `Rc<RefCell<_>>`wrapper.
- [repeat_](https://docs.rs/fn.repeat_n.html)- n
- Create an iterator that produces `n`repetitions of`element`.
- [rev](https://docs.rs/fn.rev.html)
- Iterate `iterable`in reverse.
- [sorted](https://docs.rs/fn.sorted.html)
- Sort all iterator elements into a new iterator in ascending order.
- [sorted_](https://docs.rs/fn.sorted_unstable.html)- unstable
- Sort all iterator elements into a new iterator in ascending order. This sort is unstable (i.e., may reorder equal elements).
- [unfold](https://docs.rs/fn.unfold.html)- Deprecated
- Creates a new unfold source with the specified closure as the “iterator function” and an initial state to eventually pass to the closure
- [zip](https://docs.rs/fn.zip.html)- Deprecated
- Converts the arguments to iterators and zips them.
- [zip_eq](https://docs.rs/fn.zip_eq.html)
- Zips two iterators but **panics**if they are not of the same length.

# log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log/^0.4.8/

## Expand description

A lightweight logging facade.

The `log` crate provides a single logging API that abstracts over the
actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided
by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging
implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

If no logging implementation is selected, the facade falls back to a “noop” implementation that ignores all log messages. The overhead in this case is very small - just an integer load, comparison and jump.

A log request consists of a *target*, a *level*, and a *body*. A target is a
string which defaults to the module path of the location of the log request,
though that default may be overridden. Logger implementations typically use
the target to filter requests based on some user configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The basic use of the log crate is through the five logging macros: [ error!](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)

`warn!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)

`info!`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)

`debug!`[where](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html)

`trace!``error!` represents the highest-priority log messages
and `trace!` the lowest. The log messages are filtered by configuring
the log level to exclude messages with a lower priority.
Each of these macros accept format strings similarly to [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.println.html)

`println!`Avoid writing expressions with side-effects in log statements. They may not be evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#in-libraries)In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided
macros to log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", "Commencing yak shaving for {yak:?}");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!("Razor located: {razor}");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(err) => {
                warn!("Unable to locate a razor: {err}, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-executables)In executables

Executables should choose a logging implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logging implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the implementation is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

The logging system may only be initialized once.

[§](https://docs.rs#structured-logging)Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature you can associate structured values
with your log records. If we take the example from before, we can include
some additional context besides what’s in the formatted message:

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", yak:serde; "Commencing yak shaving");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!(razor; "Razor located");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(e) => {
                warn!(e:err; "Unable to locate a razor, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
See the [ kv](https://docs.rs/kv/index.html) module documentation for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#available-logging-implementations)Available logging implementations

In order to produce log output executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some of the most popular ones:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over `log`to initialize in your libraries

- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over
- Utilities:

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-a-logger)Implementing a Logger

Loggers implement the [ Log](https://docs.rs/trait.Log.html) trait. Here’s a very basic example that simply
logs all messages at the

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Error`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Warn`[levels to stdout:](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Info````
use log::{Record, Level, Metadata};
struct SimpleLogger;
impl log::Log for SimpleLogger {
    fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
        metadata.level() <= Level::Info
    }
    fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
        if self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
            println!("{} - {}", record.level(), record.args());
        }
    }
    fn flush(&self) {}
}
```
Loggers are installed by calling the [ set_logger](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html) function. The maximum
log level also needs to be adjusted via the

[function. The logging facade uses this as an optimization to improve performance of log messages at levels that are disabled. It’s important to set it, as it defaults to](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level`[, so no log messages will ever be captured! In the case of our example logger, we’ll want to set the maximum log level to](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Off`[, since we ignore any](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Info`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Debug`[level log messages. A logging implementation should provide a function that wraps a call to](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Trace`[and](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html)

`set_logger`[, handling initialization of the logger:](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level````
use log::{SetLoggerError, LevelFilter};
static LOGGER: SimpleLogger = SimpleLogger;
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_logger(&LOGGER)
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
Implementations that adjust their configurations at runtime should take care to adjust the maximum log level as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-with-std)Use with `std`

`set_logger` requires you to provide a `&'static Log`, which can be hard to
obtain if your logger depends on some runtime configuration. The
`set_boxed_logger` function is available with the `std` Cargo feature. It is
identical to `set_logger` except that it takes a `Box<Log>` rather than a
`&'static Log`:

```
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(SimpleLogger))
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-filters)Compile time filters

Log levels can be statically disabled at compile time by enabling one of these Cargo features:

- `max_level_off`
- `max_level_error`
- `max_level_warn`
- `max_level_info`
- `max_level_debug`
- `max_level_trace`

Log invocations at disabled levels will be skipped and will not even be present in the
resulting binary. These features control the value of the `STATIC_MAX_LEVEL` constant. The
logging macros check this value before logging a message. By default, no levels are disabled.

It is possible to override this level for release builds only with the following features:

- `release_max_level_off`
- `release_max_level_error`
- `release_max_level_warn`
- `release_max_level_info`
- `release_max_level_debug`
- `release_max_level_trace`

Libraries should avoid using the max level features because they’re global and can’t be changed once they’re set.

For example, a crate can disable trace level logs in debug builds and trace, debug, and info level logs in release builds with the following configuration:

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["max_level_debug", "release_max_level_warn"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

The following crate feature flags are available in addition to the filters. They are
configured in your `Cargo.toml`.

- `std`allows use of- `std`crate instead of the default- `core`. Enables using- `std::error`and- `set_boxed_logger`functionality.
- `serde`enables support for serialization and deserialization of- `Level`and- `LevelFilter`.

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std", "serde"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#version-compatibility)Version compatibility

The 0.3 and 0.4 versions of the `log` crate are almost entirely compatible. Log messages
made using `log` 0.3 will forward transparently to a logger implementation using `log` 0.4. Log
messages made using `log` 0.4 will forward to a logger implementation using `log` 0.3, but the
module path and file name information associated with the message will unfortunately be lost.

# object - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/object/^0.36.5/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#object)`object`

The `object` crate provides a unified interface to working with object files
across platforms. It supports reading relocatable object files and executable files,
and writing relocatable object files and some executable files.

[§](https://docs.rs#raw-struct-definitions)Raw struct definitions

Raw structs are defined for: [ELF](https://docs.rs/elf/index.html), [Mach-O](https://docs.rs/macho/index.html), [PE/COFF](https://docs.rs/pe/index.html),
[XCOFF](https://docs.rs/xcoff/index.html), [archive](https://docs.rs/archive/index.html).
Types and traits for zerocopy support are defined in the [ pod](https://docs.rs/pod/index.html) and

[modules.](https://docs.rs/endian/index.html)

`endian`[§](https://docs.rs#unified-read-api)Unified read API

The [ read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html) module provides a unified read API using the

[trait. There is an implementation of this trait for](https://docs.rs/read/trait.Object.html)

`read::Object`[, which allows reading any file format, as well as implementations for each file format.](https://docs.rs/read/enum.File.html)

`read::File`[§](https://docs.rs#low-level-read-api)Low level read API

The [ read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html#modules) submodules define helpers that operate on the raw structs.
These can be used instead of the unified API, or in conjunction with it to access
details that are not available via the unified API.

[§](https://docs.rs#unified-write-api)Unified write API

The [ write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html) module provides a unified write API for relocatable object files
using

[. This does not support writing executable files.](https://docs.rs/write/struct.Object.html)

`write::Object`[§](https://docs.rs#low-level-write-api)Low level write API

The [ write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html#modules) submodules define helpers for writing the raw structs.

[§](https://docs.rs#build-api)Build API

The [ build](https://docs.rs/build/index.html) submodules define helpers for building object files, either from
scratch or by modifying existing files.

[§](https://docs.rs#shared-definitions)Shared definitions

The crate provides a number of definitions that are used by both the read and write APIs. These are defined at the top level module, but none of these are the main entry points of the crate.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [archive](https://docs.rs/archive/index.html)
- Archive definitions.
- [build](https://docs.rs/build/index.html)
- Interface for building object files.
- [elf](https://docs.rs/elf/index.html)
- ELF definitions.
- [endian](https://docs.rs/endian/index.html)
- Types for compile-time and run-time endianness.
- [macho](https://docs.rs/macho/index.html)
- Mach-O definitions.
- [pe](https://docs.rs/pe/index.html)
- PE/COFF definitions.

- Tools for converting file format structures to and from bytes.
- [read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html)
- Interface for reading object files.
- [write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html)

- [xcoff](https://docs.rs/xcoff/index.html)
- XCOFF definitions

# smallvec 1.15.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/smallvec/^1.6.1/

docs.rs failed to build smallvec-1.15.2

Please check the

See

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/smallvec/1.15.2/builds)for more information.See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).# rust-smallvec

"Small vector" optimization for Rust: store up to a small number of items on the stack

## Example

```
use ;

// This SmallVec can hold up to 4 items on the stack:
let mut v:  = smallvec!;
// It will automatically move its contents to the heap if
// contains more than four items:
v.push;
// SmallVec points to a slice, so you can use normal slice
// indexing and other methods to access its contents:
v = v + v;
v.sort;
```

# thiserror - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/thiserror/^2.0.12/

## Expand description

This library provides a convenient derive macro for the standard library’s
[ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/error/trait.Error.html) trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use thiserror::Error;
#[derive(Error, Debug)]
pub enum DataStoreError {
    #[error("data store disconnected")]
    Disconnect(#[from] io::Error),
    #[error("the data for key `{0}` is not available")]
    Redaction(String),
    #[error("invalid header (expected {expected:?}, found {found:?})")]
    InvalidHeader {
        expected: String,
        found: String,
    },
    #[error("unknown data store error")]
    Unknown,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

-
Thiserror deliberately does not appear in your public API. You get the same thing as if you had written an implementation of `std::error::Error`
-
Errors may be enums, structs with named fields, tuple structs, or unit structs.
-
A `Display``#[error("...")]`messages on the struct or each variant of your enum, as shown above in the example.The messages support a shorthand for interpolating fields from the error. - `#[error("{var}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.0)`
- `#[error("{var:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.0)`
 These shorthands can be used together with any additional format args, which may be arbitrary expressions. For example: `#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("invalid rdo_lookahead_frames {0} (expected < {max})", max = i32::MAX)] InvalidLookahead(u32), }`If one of the additional expression arguments needs to refer to a field of the struct or enum, then refer to named fields as `.var`and tuple fields as`.0`.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("first letter must be lowercase but was {:?}", first_char(.0))] WrongCase(String), #[error("invalid index {idx}, expected at least {} and at most {}", .limits.lo, .limits.hi)] OutOfBounds { idx: usize, limits: Limits }, }`
-
A `From``#[from]`attribute.The variant using `#[from]`must not contain any other fields beyond the source error (and possibly a backtrace — see below). Usually`#[from]`fields are unnamed, but`#[from]`is allowed on a named field too.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io(#[from] io::Error), Glob(#[from] globset::Error), }`
-
The Error trait’s `source()``#[source]`attribute or is named`source`, if any. This is for identifying the underlying lower level error that caused your error.The `#[from]`attribute always implies that the same field is`#[source]`, so you don’t ever need to specify both attributes.Any error type that implements `std::error::Error`or dereferences to`dyn std::error::Error`will work as a source.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, #[source] // optional if field name is `source` source: anyhow::Error, }`
-
The Error trait’s `provide()``Backtrace`, if any, as a`std::backtrace::Backtrace``Backtrace`in errors requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`use std::backtrace::Backtrace; #[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, backtrace: Backtrace, // automatically detected }`
-
If a field is both a source (named `source`, or has`#[source]`or`#[from]`attribute)*and*is marked`#[backtrace]`, then the Error trait’s`provide()``provide`so that both layers of the error share the same backtrace. The`#[backtrace]`attribute requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[backtrace] source: io::Error, }, }`
-
For variants that use `#[from]`and also contain a`Backtrace`field, a backtrace is captured from within the`From`impl.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[from] source: io::Error, backtrace: Backtrace, }, }`
-
Errors may use `error(transparent)`to forward the source and`Display``#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { ... #[error(transparent)] Other(#[from] anyhow::Error), // source and Display delegate to anyhow::Error }`Another use case is hiding implementation details of an error representation behind an opaque error type, so that the representation is able to evolve without breaking the crate’s public API. `// PublicError is public, but opaque and easy to keep compatible. #[derive(Error, Debug)] #[error(transparent)] pub struct PublicError(#[from] ErrorRepr); impl PublicError { // Accessors for anything we do want to expose publicly. } // Private and free to change across minor version of the crate. #[derive(Error, Debug)] enum ErrorRepr { ... }`
-
See also the `anyhow`

---

# wasmparser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmparser/^0.233.0/

## Expand description

A simple event-driven library for parsing WebAssembly binary files (or streams).

The parser library reports events as they happen and only stores parsing information for a brief period of time, making it very fast and memory-efficient. The event-driven model, however, has some drawbacks. If you need random access to the entire WebAssembly data-structure, this is not the right library for you. You could however, build such a data-structure using this library.

To get started, create a [ Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html) using

[and then follow the examples documented for](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.new)

`Parser::new`[or](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.parse)

`Parser::parse`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.parse_all)

`Parser::parse_all`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [collections](https://docs.rs/collections/index.html)- `validate`
- Type definitions for maps and sets used by the `wasmparser`crate.
- [component_](https://docs.rs/component_types/index.html)- types - `validate`and- `component-model`
- Types relating to type information provided by validation.
- [names](https://docs.rs/names/index.html)- `validate`and- `component-model`
- Definitions of name-related helpers and newtypes, primarily for the component model.
- [types](https://docs.rs/types/index.html)- `validate`
- Types relating to type information provided by validation.

- Used to implement the `VisitSimdOperator`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromReader.html)- Reader
- A trait implemented for items that can be decoded directly from a
`BinaryReader`, or that which can be parsed from the WebAssembly binary format.
- [Module](https://docs.rs/trait.ModuleArity.html)- Arity
- To compute the arity (param and result counts) of “variable-arity” operators, the operator_arity macro needs information about the module’s types and the current control stack. The ModuleArity trait exposes this information.
- [Subsection](https://docs.rs/trait.Subsection.html)
- A trait implemented for subsections of another outer section.
- [Visit](https://docs.rs/trait.VisitOperator.html)- Operator
- Trait implemented by types that can visit all `Operator`
- [Visit](https://docs.rs/trait.VisitSimdOperator.html)- Simd - Operator - `simd`
- Trait implemented by types that can visit all Wasm `simd`and`relaxed-simd``Operator`
- [Wasm](https://docs.rs/trait.WasmModuleResources.html)- Module - Resources - `validate`
- Types that qualify as Wasm validation database.

- [validate](https://docs.rs/fn.validate.html)- `validate`
- Test whether the given buffer contains a valid WebAssembly module or component,
analogous to `WebAssembly.validate`

# wasmtime_environ - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime-environ/=34.0.2/

## Expand description

Internal dependency of the `wasmtime` crate.

This crate is responsible for defining types and basic runtime structures
used by the `wasmtime` crate. This additionally defines primitives of
compilation and what compilers are expected to emit.

If you don’t already know what this crate is you probably want to use
`wasmtime`, not this crate.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [object](https://docs.rs/object/0.36.7/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/object/index.html);
- `pub use`- [wasmparser](https://docs.rs/wasmparser/0.233.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasmparser/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [__core](https://docs.rs/__core/index.html)
- The Rust Core Library
- [component](https://docs.rs/component/index.html)
- Support for the component model in Wasmtime.
- [drc](https://docs.rs/drc/index.html)
- Layout of Wasm GC objects in the deferred reference-counting collector.
- [fact](https://docs.rs/fact/index.html)
- Wasmtime’s Fused Adapter Compiler of Trampolines (FACT)
- [null](https://docs.rs/null/index.html)
- Layout of Wasm GC objects in the null garbage collector.
- [obj](https://docs.rs/obj/index.html)
- Utilities for working with object files that operate as Wasmtime’s serialization and intermediate format for compiled modules.
- [packed_](https://docs.rs/packed_option/index.html)- option
- Compact representation of `Option<T>`for types with a reserved value.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Rust module prelude for Wasmtime crates.

# wasmtime_math - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime-math/=34.0.2/

## Expand description

A minimal helper crate for implementing float-related operations for WebAssembly in terms of the native platform primitives.

This crate is intended to assist with solving the portability issues such as:

- Functions like `f32::trunc`are not available in`#![no_std]`targets.
- The `f32::trunc`function is likely faster than the`libm`fallback.
- Behavior of `f32::trunc`differs across platforms, for example it’s different on Windows and glibc on Linux. Additionally riscv64’s implementation of`libm`seems to have different NaN behavior than other platforms.
- Some wasm functions are in the Rust standard library, but not stable yet.

There are a few locations throughout the codebase that these functions are needed so they’re implemented only in a single location here rather than multiple.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [f32_](https://docs.rs/fn.f32_cvt_to_int_bounds.html)- cvt_ - to_ - int_ - bounds
- Returns the bounds for guarding a trapping f32-to-int conversion.
- [f64_](https://docs.rs/fn.f64_cvt_to_int_bounds.html)- cvt_ - to_ - int_ - bounds
- Same as `f32_cvt_to_int_bounds`

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# bevy_3d_tiles - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bevy_3d_tiles/0.1.1/bevy_3d_tiles/

## Expand description

3D Tiles 1.1 streaming plugin (BEVY-3D-TILES-PLAN, phases T0/T1).

One traversal engine for tiled meshes (T0/T1), point clouds (T2), and splats (T3) — the generalization of the basemap streamer’s proven selection/fetch machinery from quadtree arithmetic to tileset-defined trees (plan D5):

- `schema`- `tileset.json`serde model.
- `archive`- `.3tz`ranged reader (tail-scan →- `@3dtilesIndex1@`→ two range-GETs per entry; D2’s one-blob-per-asset artifact).
- `traversal`
- `fetch`
- `content`
- this module — ECS wiring: per-frame selection, the request scheduler (priorities recomputed each frame, out-of-cut requests aborted), time-boxed content spawning, visibility cut, eviction, and the attach/detach surface the asset loader drives (D6).

**Anchoring (T1)**: a tileset attaches to an *anchor entity* — the twin
entity (ENU placement + per-frame twin transform) or a preview root. The
tileset’s root entity is parented under the anchor with the rendition
correction as its local transform, so tiles inherit world placement the
exact way whole-file scenes do. Selection math runs in the tileset’s local
frame: the camera is pulled into that frame per set, which keeps SSE exact
under rigid/uniform anchor transforms without rebuilding tree volumes.
Dev-trigger tilesets (`TT_TILES3D=…` / `?tiles3d=…`) stay world-anchored.

[§](https://docs.rs#error-convention-public-sdk-surface)Error convention (public SDK surface)

Public fallible APIs return `thiserror` types, never `String`/`anyhow`:
[ fetch::FetchError](https://docs.rs/fetch/enum.FetchError.html) (with cancellation as the distinct

[variant — callers treat an abort differently from a failure),](https://docs.rs/fetch/enum.FetchError.html#variant.Aborted)

`fetch::FetchError::Aborted`[, and](https://docs.rs/archive/enum.ArchiveError.html)

`archive::ArchiveError`[(staged: permanent content failures vs environmental transcoder-shim failures). Internal helpers may pass plain](https://docs.rs/content/struct.DecodeError.html)

`content::DecodeError``String` messages; the typed boundary is the public function signature.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use api::`- [PointTileMaterial](https://docs.rs/api/struct.PointTileMaterial.html);
- `pub use api::`- [EcefOrigin](https://docs.rs/api/struct.EcefOrigin.html);
- `pub use api::`- [TileFeatureResolver](https://docs.rs/api/struct.TileFeatureResolver.html);
- `pub use api::`- [TileOwner](https://docs.rs/api/struct.TileOwner.html);
- `pub use api::`- [Tiles3dCamera](https://docs.rs/api/struct.Tiles3dCamera.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [api](https://docs.rs/api/index.html)
- Public, backend-agnostic API surface for `bevy_3d_tiles`.
- [archive](https://docs.rs/archive/index.html)
- `.3tz`ranged reader (BEVY-3D-TILES-PLAN T0, decision D2).
- [content](https://docs.rs/content/index.html)
- Tile content decode: GLB bytes → renderable data for the three content
types (plan D5) — triangle meshes (T0/T1), point clouds (T2), Gaussian
splats (T3). One decoder, three outputs, feeding the existing renderers
(`Mesh3d`, vendored`PointCloud`,`PlanarGaussian3d`).
- [draco](https://docs.rs/draco/index.html)
- Platform Draco decode for `KHR_draco_mesh_compression`tile content (BEVY-3D-TILES T4 — Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles ship Draco-compressed meshes; no published pure-Rust decoder exists yet, 2026-06 survey).
- [fetch](https://docs.rs/fetch/index.html)
- Byte-source IO for 3D Tiles content (BEVY-3D-TILES-PLAN T0).
- [geo](https://docs.rs/geo/index.html)
- Georeferenced-tileset geometry (BEVY-3D-TILES T4).
- [geodesy](https://docs.rs/geodesy/index.html)
- Minimal WGS84 geodesy — the only math `bevy_3d_tiles`needs to georeference ECEF/region tilesets. Pure textbook formulas (no external crate, no STDB dependency); inlined from TurboTwin’s`turbotwin_sdk_rs::enu`so the crate is self-contained. Besides geodetic→ECEF and the radius constant used in horizon culling,`world_from_ecef``crate::EcefOrigin`
- [meshopt](https://docs.rs/meshopt/index.html)
- Pure-Rust `EXT_meshopt_compression`decoder for tile content (BEVY-3D-TILES T6, decision D12 — we EMIT meshopt, never Draco, and decode it on the CPU).
- [schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)
- Serde model for 3D Tiles 1.1 `tileset.json`(BEVY-3D-TILES-PLAN T0).
- [traversal](https://docs.rs/traversal/index.html)
- Tile-tree model + the per-frame selection algorithm (BEVY-3D-TILES-PLAN §7).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Active](https://docs.rs/struct.ActiveTileset.html)- Tileset
- One streaming tileset.
- [P3dt](https://docs.rs/struct.P3dtParams.html)- Params
- Google P3DT per-layer config, denormalized from the project row (L3).
- [Tiles3d](https://docs.rs/struct.Tiles3dAttach.html)- Attach
- Attach a streaming tileset under an anchor entity (D6 resolver routing —
sent by the asset loader for `"3dtiles"`renditions, and by the layers resolver for world layers).
- [Tiles3d](https://docs.rs/struct.Tiles3dConfig.html)- Config
- [Tiles3d](https://docs.rs/struct.Tiles3dDetach.html)- Detach
- Tear down any tileset anchored to this entity (rebind / mode switch). Despawning the anchor outright works too — sets garbage-collect when their root entity dies with the hierarchy.
- [Tiles3d](https://docs.rs/struct.Tiles3dPlugin.html)- Plugin
- [Tiles3d](https://docs.rs/struct.Tiles3dSets.html)- Sets
- Live tilesets + scheduler counters.
- [Tiles3d](https://docs.rs/struct.Tiles3dTile.html)- Tile
- Marker on each spawned tile root entity.
- [Tileset](https://docs.rs/struct.TilesetCredits.html)- Credits
- Attribution side-band of the streaming tilesets, read by the basemap’s overlay system: aggregated tile copyrights (P3DT ToS requires showing them) and whether Google content is on screen (logo requirement).

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [GOOGLE_](https://docs.rs/constant.GOOGLE_P3DT_ROOT_URL.html)- P3DT_ - ROOT_ - URL
- The Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles root tileset (D7). The org’s API key is appended per request, never stored in the row.

# rsclaw-jobs 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rsclaw-jobs/0.1.0

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/rsclaw-jobs/0.1.0/builds)for more information.

See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or

[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).

`rsclaw-jobs` — pure provider-API job layer for async video / image
generation (crate-split, step-12 P2).

Lifted out of `gateway/external_jobs_worker.rs`: the per-provider HTTP
adapters (`submit_*` for the tool side, `poll_*` + `download_artifact`
for the worker side). This crate has NO gateway dependency — it knows
nothing about the task queue, `ExternalJob` persistence, channels, or
shutdown. The gateway-coupled `ExternalJobsWorker` tick/delivery loop
stays in root and calls back into these functions.

This breaks the old agent->gateway edge: `agent::tools_video` now calls
`rsclaw_jobs::submit_*` instead of reaching into the gateway worker.

Adding a new async provider means: add the corresponding `submit_*` for
the tool side and `poll_*` for the worker side, then extend the
`dispatch_poll` match in the gateway worker.

---

# hanzo-kernel 0.2.6 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/hanzo-kernel/0.2.6

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/hanzo-kernel/0.2.6/builds)for more information.

See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or

[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).

hanzo-kernel: Hanzo's first-party GPU kernel DSL.

Write a kernel ONCE in Rust; it lowers to CUDA / ROCm / Vulkan / Metal. This crate is the
first-party facade over the CubeCL lowering engine: kernel source names only `hanzo_kernel::*`,
never `cubecl`. "Values, not places" -- CubeCL is the implementation value; `hanzo_kernel` is the
stable namespace we build against, so the engine can be upgraded (or forked) without touching a
single kernel.

The perf primitives our hand-tuned kernels rely on are all here and lower to the native instruction on each backend:

- `dot`on a vectorized- `Line<i8>`-> dp4a / OpSDotAccSat (int8 4-way dot)
- `cmma`-> tensor cores (WMMA / cooperative-matrix / simdgroup)
- `SharedMemory`,- `plane_*`(subgroup reduce/shuffle),- `Atomic`, barriers

MIGRATION POLICY (perf-gated, never a downgrade): the DSL provides COVERAGE -- every quant type on every backend, from one source, killing the "same op, N impls, N numeric behaviors" bug class. A hand-tuned kernel is replaced by its DSL twin ONLY when the DSL version is bit-exact AND within perf noise (bench-gated). Where a hand-tuned kernel still wins, it stays as the specialized peak path and the DSL is the portable fallback for the backends that lack a tuned version.

# sim_lib_lang_scheme - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-lang-scheme/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_lang_scheme/

## Expand description

Scheme (R7RS-small) surface profile for the SIM runtime.

The kernel defines the codec, eval-policy, and `Expr` contracts; this crate
is a loadable language profile presenting a Scheme surface syntax over the
shared `Expr` graph, not a standalone interpreter.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Located](https://docs.rs/struct.LocatedSchemeLowering.html)- Scheme - Lowering
- A `SchemeLowered`
- [Scheme](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemeBaseExport.html)- Base - Export
- A Scheme base-library export: a surface symbol and its description.
- [Scheme](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemeCodec.html)- Codec
- Decoder turning Scheme surface text into the shared `Expr`graph.
- [Scheme](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemeCodecLib.html)- Codec - Lib
- Loadable `Lib``SchemeCodec`
- [Scheme](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemeFormSpec.html)- Form - Spec
- Specification of one R7RS-small surface form: its symbol, doc, match shape, and support status.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Scheme](https://docs.rs/enum.SchemeFormStatus.html)- Form - Status
- Whether a Scheme surface form is supported by this profile.
- [Scheme](https://docs.rs/enum.SchemeLowered.html)- Lowered
- Result of lowering a Scheme `Expr`to a runtime value.

- Lowers a located Scheme tree, preserving its origin.

# a3s 0.6.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/a3s/0.6.0

# a3s

The umbrella CLI for the [A3S](https://github.com/A3S-Lab) platform.

`a3s <tool> [args...]` runs the matching A3S tool. `a3s box ...` proxies to
`a3s-box ...` and bootstraps the Box runtime automatically if it is missing:

```
a3s code            # → a3s-code   (launches its TUI)
a3s box ps          # → a3s-box ps (auto-installs a3s-box if needed)
a3s <tool> --help   # a tool's own help
a3s list            # list installed a3s-* tools
a3s --version
```
## Install

```
# from source
# or from this repo
# or Homebrew
```
Then run the tools you need. `a3s box ...` installs `a3s-box` on first use.

## Account Models

In `a3s code`, `/model` lists configured `config.acl` models plus signed-in
account tabs. When Claude Code is logged in (`claude /login`), the Claude Code
tab can switch the current session to Claude models using the local Claude Code
OAuth credentials, including Claude Code's macOS Keychain entry.
`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` or `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` can also provide the account
token for non-standard environments. If Anthropic rejects the raw OAuth Messages
API bridge with a rate-limit or authentication error, a3s falls back to the
installed `claude` CLI in safe streaming mode; Claude Code's own tools stay
disabled while a3s host tools are requested through an adapter protocol and
still execute inside a3s-code. The adapter accepts Claude Code-style
`<function_calls>` output and tool names such as `Read` or `Bash`, normalizes
common argument aliases like `path` to a3s's `file_path`, and feeds tool results
back into the next Claude turn as structured history.

## Testing

```
```
The ignored soak test repeats `a3s box` after a fake first-use install and
verifies later runs reuse the installed `a3s-box`. The ignored
`ctx_compact_real_llm` test drives the configured model (`~/.a3s/config.acl`)
until the context crosses the auto-compact threshold and asserts streaming
usage is reported, compaction shrinks the history, and the next prompt drops —
the machinery behind the TUI's ctx%, fill warnings, and auto-compaction.

## Updating

In the TUI, ** /update** upgrades to the latest release and restarts into your
session — Homebrew installs are refreshed + upgraded; standalone installs swap
the binary directly. Both paths verify the installed binary reports the target
version before treating the update as successful.

If you're on an **older build (≤ 0.5.4)** whose `/update` was broken, it can't
upgrade itself, and `brew upgrade a3s` alone won't see the new version (Homebrew
doesn't re-sync a tap on `upgrade`). Bootstrap onto a current build once with:

```
 &&
```
From 0.5.5 onward, `/update` handles the tap refresh itself, so this manual step
isn't needed again.

## License

MIT
